title: Chapter XXXVI

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth rereads the letter, recognizes that she has been prejudiced and blind, and exclaims, 'Till this moment I never knew myself.'

vocabulary.context: His attentions to Miss King were now the consequence of views solely and hatefully mercenary; and the mediocrity of her fortune proved no longer the moderation of his wishes, but his eagerness to grasp at anything.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “hateful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Weighing facts and arguments with a view a choice or decision
vocabulary.context: She put down the letter, weighed every circumstance with what she meant to be impartiality—deliberated on the probability of each statement—but with little success.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deliberate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + lib (Latin liber, "free" / "book") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To act as a friend to
vocabulary.context: But no such recollection befriended her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “befriend”: be- (Old English be-, "thoroughly, about"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: But when she read, and reread with the closest attention, the particulars immediately following of Wickham’s resigning all pretensions to the living, of his receiving in lieu, so considerable a sum as three thousand pounds, again was she forced to hesitate.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “resign”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A game of chance played with dice
vocabulary.context: Darcy would never have hazarded such a proposal, if he had not been well assured of his cousin’s corroboration.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “hazard”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were concerned.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “court”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of deserving well or ill
vocabulary.context: When she came to that part of the letter in which her family were mentioned, in terms of such mortifying, yet merited reproach, her sense of shame was severe.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “merit”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Feeling pain or sorrow on account of sins or offenses
vocabulary.context: He expressed no regret for what he had done which satisfied her; his style was not penitent, but haughty.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “penitent”: -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: She remembered that he had boasted of having no fear of seeing Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “boast”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: The extravagance and general profligacy which he scrupled not to lay to Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “extravagance”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + vag (Latin vagari, "to wander") + -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Moral self-examination drew on Enlightenment ideals of reason over prejudice.

significance: The turning point of the novel: Elizabeth's self-knowledge.
discussionQuestions: What exactly does Elizabeth realize about herself?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXVI,” how does Austen show self-recognition? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXVI develops the idea of self-recognition. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXXVI to complicate the reader's understanding of self-recognition. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of self-recognition responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of self-recognition. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “How despicably have I acted!” she cried. “I, who have prided myself on my discernment!—I, who have valued myself on my abilities! who have often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my vanity, in useless or blameable distrust. How humiliating is this discovery!—Yet, how just a humiliation!—Had I been in love, I could not have been more wretchedly blind. But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were concerned. Till this moment, I never knew myself.”

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What exactly does Elizabeth realize about herself? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are hatefully, deliberated, befriended, resigning, hazarded. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “His attentions to Miss King were now the consequence of views solely and hatefully mercenary; and the mediocrity of her fortune proved no longer the moderation of his wishes, but his eagerness to grasp at anything.” Webster's says: Manifesting hate or hatred. Now the word history: “hateful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “deliberate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + lib (Latin liber, "free" / "book") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “befriend”: be- (Old English be-, "thoroughly, about"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Moral self-examination drew on Enlightenment ideals of reason over prejudice. Why does this chapter matter? The turning point of the novel: Elizabeth's self-knowledge. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to self-recognition.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
